tool.name: Django
tool.tagline: Batteries-included Python web framework: ORM, admin, auth, forms and templates
tool.description: Django is a full-stack Python web framework that ships with an ORM and migrations, an automatic admin, authentication, forms, templates, caching and security protections out of the box. Its conventions let teams build database-backed sites and APIs quickly and keep them maintainable for years. It powers sites such as Instagram and countless business applications.

glossary.def: The whole Django site: its settings, its top-level list of URLs and the files a server loads to start it. A project contains one or more apps.
One self-contained feature of a Django site, such as a blog or user accounts, in its own folder with its own data definitions, views and templates.
A small script in every Django project that runs Django commands (start the dev server, update the database, run tests) with that project's settings loaded.
The list in a Django project's settings naming every app the site uses. Django ignores an app's models and templates until it is listed here.
In Django, the Python function (or class) that handles one kind of request: it receives the request and returns the response, such as a finished HTML page.
In Django, the list (called urlpatterns, in a urls.py file) that says which view runs for which URL.
A marker like <int:pk> inside a Django URL pattern that captures that part of the URL, converts it (here to an integer) and passes it to the view.
A short, URL-friendly label made of lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, such as my-first-post, used in page addresses instead of a number.
The dictionary of values a Django view hands to a template; the template's placeholders are filled from it.
A {% ... %} instruction in a Django template that does something, such as a loop, an if, or building a link.
A |name added to a value in a Django template to change how it is shown, such as {{ title|upper }} or {{ date|date:"Y-m-d" }}.
Writing a page layout once in a base template with named gaps (blocks), then having each page extend it and fill only the gaps it changes.
Automatically turning characters like < and & in a value into harmless codes before it goes into a page, so text a user typed is shown as text and never runs as code.
In Django, files your users upload (such as profile photos), stored separately from the site's own static files because they can't be trusted.
In Django, a Python class that describes one database table: each field attribute is a column and each instance is a row.
The object on a Django model (usually called objects) that starts database queries, as in Post.objects.filter(...).
In Django, a description of a database query that you can keep refining (filter, sort, slice). It runs only when you actually use the results.
The part after a double underscore in a Django filter that says how to compare, as in title__icontains="django" (contains, ignoring case) or views__gte=100 (at least 100).
The required option on a Django ForeignKey that decides what happens to rows pointing at a row that gets deleted: delete them too, block the deletion, or empty the link.
The option on a Django relationship field that names the way back, so author.posts.all() lists an author's posts.
Django's built-in back office: web pages, generated from your models, where trusted staff can browse, search and edit the site's data.
A class in a Django app's admin.py that customises how one model appears in the admin: which columns, filters, search box and edit form it gets.
In Django, a user account with every permission, typically created with manage.py createsuperuser to log in to the admin.
In Django, a user allowed to log in to the admin site (is_staff is on). What they can see and change there depends on their permissions.
In the Django admin, a small table of related objects (such as a post's comments) edited directly on the parent object's page.
In the Django admin, a function you can run on all the rows you have ticked in a list, such as 'publish selected posts'.
A Python class listing the fields a web form has; Django uses it to draw the HTML form, check what users submit and convert it into Python values.
A Django form that has been given submitted data to check (bound), as opposed to an empty form just for display (unbound).
The dictionary a Django form fills after is_valid() succeeds: every submitted value, checked and converted to the right Python type.
In a Django form, the piece that decides which HTML input a field is drawn as, such as a one-line text box or a multi-line Textarea.
A Django form that builds its fields from a model and can save the result straight to the database as a new or updated row.
A security hole where a form or API lets users set fields they were never meant to change, such as is_staff or price, just by sending extra values.
A Django view written as a class instead of a function; you customise it by setting attributes and overriding methods.
One of Django's ready-made class-based views for common pages (a list, one object's detail, a create or edit form, a delete confirmation).
In Django, a named right such as blog.change_post (may edit posts). Each model gets add, change, delete and view permissions; users get them directly or through groups.
In Django's auth system, a named set of permissions (like 'Editors'); every user in the group gets them.
In Django, a wrapper around one filter condition so conditions can be combined with | (or), & (and) and ~ (not).
In Django, F("column") means 'the value already in this column', so the database itself can compare or update it, as in views = F("views") + 1.
In Django, a value computed by the database and attached to every object a QuerySet returns, such as each author's number of posts.
A Django QuerySet method that loads linked objects (through ForeignKey or OneToOne) in the same query, using a SQL JOIN.
A Django QuerySet method that loads many-valued links (many-to-many, or an author's posts) with one extra query per link and matches them up in Python.
Your own subclass of Django's QuerySet with named query methods (like published()), so a filter you use everywhere is written once and can be chained.
A long random Django setting used to sign data the site hands out (session cookies, password-reset links) so forgeries are detected. It must stay secret.
A Django setting listing the domain names the site answers to; requests for any other name are refused.
In Django tests, a pretend browser (self.client) that sends requests through your whole app, without a real server, and returns the responses for checking.
In Django, code wrapped in transaction.atomic(): all its database writes are kept together and committed at the end, or all undone if an error escapes.
A Django function that runs a piece of code only once the current transaction has been committed, and never if it is rolled back.
A Django QuerySet method that locks the rows it reads until the transaction ends, so no other request can change them in between.
In Django, an announcement such as 'a Post was just saved' that any number of functions (receivers) can subscribe to and react to.
In Django, a function connected to a signal; it runs every time that signal is sent.
The class in a Django app's apps.py describing the app; its ready() method runs once at startup and is the place to connect signal receivers.
The Django setting naming the model that represents users (such as "accounts.User"); other models link to users through it.
An attack where another site shows your page inside an invisible frame and tricks visitors into clicking buttons on it.
A response header telling browsers to use only the encrypted https:// version of a site for a set time, even if someone types http://.
A response header listing where a page may load scripts, styles and images from, so the browser refuses anything an attacker sneaked in.
A random value made fresh for each response; a Content Security Policy can allow only the inline scripts that carry it.
In Django, the storage that holds cached values: process memory, a file, a database table, or a separate service such as Redis.
A fast database that keeps its data in memory and stores values under keys; widely used as a shared cache and for job queues.
In Django, caching just one part of a rendered page (with the {% cache %} tag), such as an expensive sidebar.
Django 6.0's built-in, standard way to declare background tasks (@task) and queue them (.enqueue()); running them for real needs a worker from a separate backend package.
A popular Python library for running background tasks in separate worker processes, which pick up jobs your app leaves in a shared store such as Redis.
The standard way a Python web app and a web server talk to each other: the server calls the app once per request and gets the response back. Django, Flask and Gunicorn all speak it.
The async successor of WSGI: a standard that lets Python web apps use async code and hold long connections such as WebSockets. Uvicorn is a common ASGI server.
A widely used production server for Python web apps that speak WSGI; it runs several copies (workers) of your app to handle requests in parallel.
A fast production server for Python web apps that speak ASGI, used for async Django, FastAPI and Starlette.

concepts.name: Projects, apps and manage.py
concepts.summary: Create a Django project, add apps with startapp, register them in INSTALLED_APPS and run the local development server.
concepts.why: The project/app structure and the manage.py commands are the frame every other Django feature lives in.
concepts.body:
When you open a page, your browser sends a request to a server, and a program on that server sends back the HTML. Django is a **web framework**: a ready-made toolkit for writing that server program in Python. You write only the parts unique to your site; Django handles receiving requests, talking to the database and building pages.

Django splits your code into one **project** and several **apps**. The project is the whole site: its settings and its top-level list of URLs. An app is one self-contained feature, such as `blog` or `accounts`, with its own data definitions, page logic and HTML files.

```bash
python -m pip install django
django-admin startproject mysite .
python manage.py startapp blog
python manage.py runserver
```

The trailing `.` puts `manage.py` in the folder your terminal is in, instead of a new subfolder. The project package `mysite/` contains:

- `settings.py`: all configuration, including `INSTALLED_APPS` (the apps the site uses) and `DATABASES` (SQLite by default, so there is nothing to install)
- `urls.py`: the site's top-level list of URLs
- `wsgi.py` and `asgi.py`: files a real server loads to start your site; you can ignore them until the site goes online

`startapp blog` creates a folder with `models.py` (data), `views.py` (page logic), `admin.py`, `apps.py`, `tests.py` and a `migrations/` package; each gets its own lesson. Django ignores the app until you add `"blog"` to `INSTALLED_APPS`. Forgetting this is the classic reason models or templates are "not found".

`manage.py` is a small script that runs Django commands with your project's settings loaded. You'll use it constantly: `runserver`, `migrate`, `createsuperuser`, `test`, `check`, and `shell` (a Python REPL with your project and models already imported).

`runserver` starts a **development server**: a small web server on your own computer, at `http://127.0.0.1:8000/`, that restarts itself whenever you save a change. A **web server** is simply a program that waits for requests and sends back pages.

The development server is not built for real traffic or attacks. Putting the site online, called **deploying** it, means running it under a proper server program; that live copy real users rely on is **production**. The Deployment lesson covers it. Django 6.0 requires Python 3.12 or newer.

Design apps around one responsibility each; small focused apps are easier to test and reuse than one giant app.
concepts.code:
# terminal
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install "django~=6.0"
django-admin startproject mysite .
python manage.py startapp blog

# mysite/settings.py  (excerpt)
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    "django.contrib.admin",
    "django.contrib.auth",
    "django.contrib.contenttypes",
    "django.contrib.sessions",
    "django.contrib.messages",
    "django.contrib.staticfiles",
    "blog",                       # your app must be listed here
]

# back in the terminal
python manage.py migrate          # create tables for the built-in apps
python manage.py runserver        # http://127.0.0.1:8000/
takeaways: A project holds settings and top-level URLs; apps hold features
Add every app to INSTALLED_APPS
manage.py runs commands with your project's settings; runserver is for development only
pitfalls: Creating an app but forgetting to add it to INSTALLED_APPS.

quiz.q: You created a new app with startapp, but Django can't find its models or templates. What is the most likely cause?
options: The app is not in INSTALLED_APPS
You need to restart your computer
quiz.explain: Django only looks for models, migrations and templates in apps listed in INSTALLED_APPS.

concepts.name: URLconfs and function views
concepts.summary: Map URLs to views with path(), capture parts of the URL, name your routes and build links from the names.
concepts.why: A view is where an incoming request becomes the page sent back, and named URLs keep links correct as the site grows.
concepts.body:
When you open a page, your browser sends the request using **HTTP**, the set of rules browsers and servers use to talk. The server always answers with a **response**: the content (usually HTML) plus a three-digit **status code** saying how it went. 200 means OK; 404 means "not found".

Every request also carries a **method** saying what it wants. `GET` means "just show me something", as when you click a link. `POST` means "here is some data for you", as when you submit a form.

In Django, the function that handles a request is a **view**. It receives an `HttpRequest` object and returns an `HttpResponse`. The **URLconf**, a list called `urlpatterns` in `urls.py`, decides which view runs for which URL:

```python
urlpatterns = [path("posts/<int:pk>/", views.post_detail, name="post-detail")]
```

`<int:pk>` captures that part of the URL, converts it to an `int` and passes it to the view as the keyword argument `pk` (short for primary key). These **path converters** come as `str`, `int`, `slug` (a URL-friendly label like `my-first-post`), `uuid` and `path`. Patterns have no leading slash and usually end with one.

Each app usually has its own `urls.py`, plugged into the project's with `path("blog/", include("blog.urls"))`. Setting `app_name = "blog"` in the app's file gives its URL names a prefix, a **namespace**, so they are written `"blog:post-detail"` and can't clash with another app's `post-detail`.

**Never type URLs by hand.** Build them from names: `reverse("blog:post-detail", args=[3])` in Python, `{% url 'blog:post-detail' post.pk %}` in templates (next lesson), and `redirect("blog:post-detail", pk=3)` to send the browser on to another page, which is called a **redirect**. Change a pattern later and every link follows.

Inside a view:

- `request.method` (`"GET"` or `"POST"`), `request.GET` and `request.POST` (the query-string or form values, in dict-like `QueryDict`s), `request.headers`, `request.user`
- return `HttpResponse`, `JsonResponse` (data as JSON), `redirect(...)` or `render(...)` (fills an HTML template)
- once you have models, `get_object_or_404(Post, pk=pk)` returns the row or answers with a 404
- raise `Http404` yourself for other not-found cases

Decorators such as `@require_POST` or `@require_http_methods(["GET", "POST"])` reject other methods with status 405 ("method not allowed").
concepts.code:
# blog/urls.py
from django.urls import path
from . import views

app_name = "blog"
urlpatterns = [
    path("", views.post_list, name="list"),
    path("posts/<int:pk>/", views.post_detail, name="detail"),
]

# blog/views.py
from django.http import Http404, JsonResponse
from django.urls import reverse

POSTS = {1: "Hello Django", 2: "URLs and views"}   # stand-in for a database table

def post_list(request):
    q = request.GET.get("q", "")                 # /blog/?q=django -> "django"
    results = [{"title": t, "url": reverse("blog:detail", args=[pk])}
               for pk, t in POSTS.items() if q.lower() in t.lower()]
    return JsonResponse({"results": results})    # status 200, JSON body

def post_detail(request, pk):                    # pk arrives as an int
    if pk not in POSTS:
        raise Http404("No such post")            # Django answers with a 404
    return JsonResponse({"title": POSTS[pk]})
# mysite/urls.py:  path("blog/", include("blog.urls"))  ->  /blog/posts/2/
takeaways: A view takes a request and returns a response; the URLconf picks the view
path("route/<int:pk>/", view, name=...) maps URLs to views
include() + app_name give each app its own namespaced URLs
Build URLs with reverse() and {% url %}, never by hand
pitfalls: Starting a pattern with a slash ("/posts/"), which never matches.

quiz.q: With app_name = "blog" and path("posts/<int:pk>/", ..., name="detail") included under "blog/", what does reverse("blog:detail", args=[7]) return?
quiz.explain: reverse joins the include prefix (blog/) with the named pattern (posts/<int:pk>/) and fills in the argument.

concepts.name: Templates and the template language
concepts.summary: Build HTML pages with render(): fill templates with variables, tags and filters, and share one layout with template inheritance.
concepts.why: Most Django sites build their HTML on the server, and templates keep that HTML readable, reusable and safe.
concepts.body:
Writing HTML inside Python strings gets messy fast. Instead, Django keeps each page in a **template**: an HTML file with placeholders that are filled in with data for each request.

`render(request, "blog/post_list.html", {"posts": posts})` loads a template, fills it from the dict you pass (the **context dict**) and returns an `HttpResponse` holding the finished HTML. Producing the finished page from template plus data is called **rendering**.

Django looks for templates in a `templates/` folder inside each installed app. All apps share one search list, so two apps' `list.html` would clash. Put the blog's templates in `blog/templates/blog/` and refer to them as `"blog/..."`: the extra folder keeps the names apart.

The Django Template Language (DTL) has three kinds of placeholder:

- `{{ post.title }}`: a variable, replaced by its value. The dot looks up a dict key, an attribute, a method without arguments or a list index.
- `{{ post.created|date:"Y-m-d" }}`: a **template filter** after `|` changes how a value is shown. Others: `|default:"none"`, `|truncatewords:30`, `|length`, `|linebreaks`.
- `{% ... %}`: a **template tag** that does something: `{% for p in posts %}...{% empty %}No posts{% endfor %}`, `{% if %}...{% elif %}...{% endif %}`, or `{% url 'blog:detail' p.pk %}` for links.

Inside every form that sends data with POST, add `{% csrf_token %}`. It inserts a hidden code proving the form came from your own site; the Security lesson explains the attack it blocks.

Most pages share a layout. Write it once in `base.html` with named gaps such as `{% block content %}{% endblock %}`, then start each page with `{% extends "base.html" %}` and fill only the gaps it changes. This is **template inheritance**. For a small snippet used on several pages, use `{% include "partials/card.html" %}`.

Django 6.0 adds template partials: `{% partialdef card %}...{% endpartialdef %}` names a fragment inside a template and `{% partial card %}` reuses it there. `render(request, "page.html#card", ...)` renders just that fragment, handy when JavaScript on the page asks for one piece to refresh.

Output is **autoescaped**: characters like `<` and `&` become character references, so a title containing `<script>` shows as text instead of running as code. `|safe` and `mark_safe` turn this off, so use them only on HTML you wrote yourself.

The DTL deliberately can't call functions with arguments or run arbitrary Python: prepare data in the view. (Django can also use Jinja, a more powerful template language, if you need one.)

Namespace templates as app/templates/app/name.html
{{ variable }}, {% tag %}, value|filter; output is autoescaped

quiz.q: Why put blog templates in blog/templates/blog/ rather than blog/templates/?
options: All apps share one template search path, so the extra folder prevents name clashes
quiz.explain: Templates from every app are searched together; the app-named folder namespaces them.

concepts.name: Static files
concepts.summary: Serve CSS, JavaScript and images with the {% static %} tag, and gather them with collectstatic when the site goes live.
concepts.why: Every site has CSS files and images, and Django handles them differently on your computer and on the live site.
concepts.body:
Some files are sent to the browser exactly as they are on disk: CSS, JavaScript, images. Django calls them **static files**, because no Python runs to produce them. The `django.contrib.staticfiles` app (installed by default) finds them in:

- each app's `static/` folder, namespaced like templates: `blog/static/blog/site.css`
- extra folders listed in `STATICFILES_DIRS`, for files the whole project uses

In templates, load the tag library and build URLs with `{% static %}`:

```html
{% load static %}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'blog/site.css' %}">
```

The URL starts with `STATIC_URL` (default `"static/"`). While you develop with `DEBUG = True` (Django's development mode, which also shows detailed error pages), `runserver` serves static files for you.

In production, Django does not serve them: a Python program is a slow way to send plain files. Run `python manage.py collectstatic`, which copies every static file into the one folder named by `STATIC_ROOT`. Then something fast sends that folder: the web server in front of Django (such as Nginx), the WhiteNoise package inside your app, or a **CDN**.

A CDN (content delivery network) is a set of servers around the world that keep copies of your files close to your users, so pages load faster.

Browsers also keep copies of files they have downloaded, so the next visit is quicker; they **cache** them. If you change `site.css`, a browser may keep using its old copy. `ManifestStaticFilesStorage` (set in `STORAGES["staticfiles"]`) fixes that: `collectstatic` gives each file a name containing a fingerprint of its contents, like `site.3f2a1c.css`. Browsers can cache it forever, and a changed file gets a new name. That only works if every link uses `{% static %}`.

**Media files** are different: files your users upload, such as profile photos. They use `MEDIA_URL` and `MEDIA_ROOT` (or an online file-storage service) and must never be mixed with static files: anyone can upload anything, so uploads can't be trusted like your own code.
concepts.code: # mysite/settings.py from pathlib import Path BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent STATIC_URL = "static/" STATICFILES_DIRS = [BASE_DIR / "assets"] # project-wide files STATIC_ROOT = BASE_DIR / "staticfiles" # collectstatic target STORAGES = { "default": {"BACKEND": "django.core.files.storage.FileSystemStorage"}, "staticfiles": {"BACKEND": "django.contrib.staticfiles.storage.ManifestStaticFilesStorage"}, } MEDIA_URL = "media/" # user uploads, kept separate MEDIA_ROOT = BASE_DIR / "media" # template: # {% load static %} # # when deploying: # python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
takeaways: App files live in app/static/app/; link them with {% static %}
collectstatic gathers files into STATIC_ROOT for the web server or CDN
Media files (user uploads) are kept separate from static files
pitfalls: Typing /static/... paths by hand, which breaks fingerprinted file names and CDN URLs.

quiz.q: What does python manage.py collectstatic do?
options: Copies all static files into STATIC_ROOT
Uploads user media to the CDN
quiz.explain: collectstatic gathers files from every app and STATICFILES_DIRS into one folder that the production web server or CDN sends out.

concepts.name: Defining models
concepts.summary: Describe database tables as Python classes with typed fields and options like null, blank, default and choices.
concepts.why: Models are the single source of truth for your data: Django builds the tables, the admin pages and the forms from them.
concepts.body:
In SQL you describe a table with `CREATE TABLE`. In Django you describe it as a Python class instead, called a **model**: a subclass of `models.Model` where each field attribute becomes a column. Django writes the SQL for you.

This translation layer is called an **ORM** (object-relational mapper): you work with rows as ordinary Python objects instead of writing SQL by hand. Field types:

- text: `CharField(max_length=200)`, `TextField()`, `EmailField()`, `URLField()`, and `SlugField()` for URL-friendly labels like `my-first-post`
- numbers: `IntegerField`, `PositiveIntegerField`, `DecimalField(max_digits=8, decimal_places=2)` for money, `FloatField`
- others: `BooleanField`, `DateField`, `DateTimeField`, `UUIDField`, `JSONField`, `FileField`, `ImageField`

Every model gets an automatic primary key `id`. In Django 6.0 it is a `BigAutoField`: an integer the database fills in, big enough for billions of rows.

Common field options:

- `null=True`: the database column allows NULL
- `blank=True`: Django's input checks accept an empty value. These checks, run by forms and the admin before saving, are called **validation**.
- `default=...`: a default filled in by Python; `db_default=...` sets it in the database instead
- `unique=True`, `db_index=True`, `verbose_name`, `help_text`
- `choices=`: limit the field to a fixed list of values, usually written as a `TextChoices` or `IntegerChoices` class inside the model (see the code). Django adds `get_<field>_display()` to show the human-readable label.

`null` and `blank` are different: one is about the database, the other about validation. For text fields, prefer `blank=True` with an empty string over `null=True`, so there is only one kind of "empty".

`DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)` sets the creation time once; `auto_now=True` updates it on every save.

Always define `__str__`: Django uses it whenever it shows an object, in the admin site, in `manage.py shell` and in error messages. Table-wide options go in an inner `class Meta`, such as `ordering` (default sort), `verbose_name_plural`, indexes and constraints.
concepts.code:
# blog/models.py
from django.db import models

class Author(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    email = models.EmailField(unique=True)

    def __str__(self):
        return self.name

class Post(models.Model):
    class Status(models.TextChoices):
        DRAFT = "draft", "Draft"
        PUBLISHED = "pub", "Published"

    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    slug = models.SlugField(unique=True)
    body = models.TextField(blank=True)
    status = models.CharField(max_length=5, choices=Status, default=Status.DRAFT)
    views = models.PositiveIntegerField(default=0)
    created = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    class Meta:
        ordering = ["-created"]
    def __str__(self):
        return self.title      # post.get_status_display() -> "Published"
takeaways: Subclass models.Model; field attributes become columns
null is about the database, blank about validation
Use TextChoices/IntegerChoices for fixed sets of values
Always define __str__
pitfalls: Using null=True on CharField/TextField, giving two kinds of empty: NULL and "".

quiz.q: Users should be allowed to leave a CharField empty when they fill it in. What do you set?
quiz.explain: blank controls validation, the checks on input before saving; null only affects the database column.

concepts.name: Migrations
concepts.summary: Turn model changes into versioned migration files with makemigrations and apply them to the database with migrate.
concepts.why: Migrations keep every developer's database and the live site's database in step with the code.
concepts.body:
Changing a model class doesn't change the database table. Django never touches your schema silently; when models change, you run two commands:

1. `python manage.py makemigrations`: compares your models with the state recorded in existing migration files and writes a new file, such as `blog/migrations/0002_post_views.py`, with steps like `AddField`.
2. `python manage.py migrate`: applies migrations that haven't run yet and records them in the `django_migrations` table.

Migration files are **code**: commit them to version control together with the model change, review them, and deploy them together. Every copy of the database, on each developer's computer and in production, then reaches the same schema by running `migrate`.

Useful commands:

- `showmigrations`: which migrations have been applied
- `sqlmigrate blog 0002`: prints the SQL a migration will run, useful for spotting a change that would lock a big table for a long time
- `migrate blog 0001`: go back to an earlier state (if the steps can be reversed)
- `makemigrations --check --dry-run`: exits with an error if someone changed models without creating a migration; add it to the automatic checks that run on every code change

When you add a required (non-null) field to a table that already has rows, `makemigrations` asks for a one-off value to fill in, or you add `default=` or `null=True` to the field.

Rules of thumb:

- never edit a migration that has already run somewhere else; create a new one
- don't delete migration files of an app that's already live
- when two developers each add a migration in separate git branches, `makemigrations --merge` creates a merge migration that joins them

Migrations also record changes that never reach the SQL, such as `choices`, so small model edits create migrations too; that's expected.
concepts.code:
# 1. change the model (blog/models.py)
#        views = models.PositiveIntegerField(default=0)

$ python manage.py makemigrations blog
Migrations for 'blog':
  blog/migrations/0002_post_views.py
    + Add field views to post

$ python manage.py sqlmigrate blog 0002          # review the SQL
$ python manage.py migrate
Applying blog.0002_post_views... OK

$ python manage.py showmigrations blog
blog

# CI: fail if models and migrations are out of sync
$ python manage.py makemigrations --check --dry-run
takeaways: makemigrations writes migration files; migrate applies them
Commit migrations with the model change
Never edit migrations that already ran elsewhere
pitfalls: Changing models and forgetting makemigrations, so the production database never gets the new column.

quiz.q: You added a field to a model. What must happen before the database has the new column?
quiz.explain: makemigrations records the change as a migration file; migrate applies it to the database.

concepts.name: Querying with QuerySets
concepts.summary: Create, read, update and delete rows from Python: filter, exclude, get, order_by, slicing and field lookups.
concepts.why: Almost every page reads or writes data, and QuerySets are how Django does it safely and readably.
concepts.body:
Each model has a **manager**, `Post.objects`, where every query starts. Its methods return **QuerySets**: descriptions of a query that you keep refining by chaining more methods, as in `Post.objects.filter(...).order_by(...)`.

Reading:

- `Post.objects.all()`, `.filter(status="pub")`, `.exclude(views=0)`
- `.get(pk=1)` returns exactly one object, or raises `Post.DoesNotExist` (none) or `MultipleObjectsReturned` (several)
- `.order_by("-created", "title")` (`-` means descending), `.first()`, `.last()`, `.count()`, `.exists()`
- slicing `[:10]` becomes `LIMIT 10`; `[10:20]` adds `OFFSET`

**Field lookups** add a condition after a double underscore: `title__icontains="django"` (contains, ignoring case), `views__gte=100` (greater than or equal), `created__year=2025`, `status__in=["pub", "draft"]`, `body__isnull=True`, `slug__startswith="how"`.

Several keyword arguments in one `filter()` are combined with AND.

Writing:

- `Post.objects.create(title=..., ...)` inserts a row and returns the object
- change attributes, then `post.save()`; `save(update_fields=["title"])` writes only those columns
- `Post.objects.filter(status="draft").update(status="pub")` runs one UPDATE without loading any objects
- `post.delete()` or `queryset.delete()`
- `get_or_create(...)` and `update_or_create(...)` find a matching row or create it, so running the code twice doesn't make duplicates

`values("title")` returns dicts and `values_list("title", flat=True)` plain values, which is cheaper when you don't need model objects.

QuerySets are **lazy**: building one runs no SQL. The query runs only when you need the results: when you loop over it, call `len()`, `list()` or `bool()`, slice it with a step, or print it.

The ORM always sends your values separately from the SQL text, so a value like `'; DROP TABLE` is treated as plain data, never as SQL. That protects you from **SQL injection**: an attack where someone types database commands into an input field, hoping the app pastes them into its SQL.
concepts.code:
from blog.models import Post

post = Post.objects.create(title="Hello Django", slug="hello", status="pub")

published = Post.objects.filter(status="pub").exclude(views=0)   # no SQL yet
recent = published.order_by("-created")[:5]                     # still lazy
for p in recent:                                                 # SQL runs here
    print(p.title)

Post.objects.filter(title__icontains="django", created__year=2025).count()
Post.objects.filter(status__in=["pub", "draft"]).exists()        # True

try:
    Post.objects.get(slug="nope")
except Post.DoesNotExist:
    print("not found")

post.title = "Hello, Django"
post.save(update_fields=["title"])
Post.objects.filter(status="draft").update(status="pub")          # one UPDATE
titles = list(Post.objects.values_list("title", flat=True))      # ['Hello, Django', ...]
print(Post.objects.filter(status="pub").query)   # SELECT ... WHERE "blog_post"."status" = pub ...
takeaways: filter/exclude/order_by chain lazily; SQL runs when you use the results
field__lookup=value expresses conditions (icontains, gte, in, year...)
get() raises DoesNotExist; update() and delete() work on whole QuerySets
pitfalls: Using get() for something that may be missing without catching DoesNotExist (in views, use get_object_or_404).

quiz.q: When does Post.objects.filter(status="pub").order_by("-created") hit the database?
options: When the page has been sent
When the QuerySet is evaluated, e.g. iterated or converted to a list
quiz.explain: QuerySets are lazy; building and chaining them doesn't run SQL until evaluation.

concepts.name: Relationships: ForeignKey and ManyToMany
concepts.summary: Link models with ForeignKey, ManyToManyField and OneToOneField, choose what deleting does, and query across the links.
concepts.why: Real data is connected, and following those connections in both directions is everyday Django work.
concepts.body:
Three field types connect models:

- **`ForeignKey`** (many-to-one): many posts belong to one author. `author = models.ForeignKey(Author, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name="posts")`. In the database this becomes a **foreign key**: a column `author_id` holding the primary key of the author's row.
- **`ManyToManyField`**: a post has many tags and a tag has many posts. Django creates the extra table that connects them, a **junction table** with one row per post-tag pair. Use `through=` to supply your own, with extra columns.
- **`OneToOneField`**: exactly one on each side, such as a `Profile` for each `User`.

These are the classic **one-to-many** and many-to-many relationships from database design.

`on_delete` is required on `ForeignKey` and decides what happens to the posts when their author is deleted:

- `CASCADE`: delete the posts too
- `PROTECT` / `RESTRICT`: refuse the deletion with an error
- `SET_NULL`: set `author_id` to NULL (the field needs `null=True`)
- `SET_DEFAULT`, `DO_NOTHING`

Following links:

- forward: `post.author` (one query the first time, then remembered on the object)
- backward: `author.posts.all()`, named by `related_name` (without it, Django calls it `author.post_set`)
- many-to-many: `post.tags.add(t)`, `.remove(t)`, `.set([...])`, `.clear()`, and `post.tags.all()`

**Query across relationships** with double underscores, in both directions:

```python
Post.objects.filter(author__name="Ann")
Author.objects.filter(posts__tags__name="django").distinct()
```

When a filter goes through a link that can match several rows (an author has many posts), the same author can come back more than once, hence `.distinct()`.

Always set `related_name`: it makes the backward link readable, and it avoids name clashes when two foreign keys point at the same model.
concepts.code:
from django.db import models

class Tag(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=50, unique=True)

class Post(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    author = models.ForeignKey("Author", on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name="posts")
    tags = models.ManyToManyField(Tag, blank=True, related_name="posts")

class Comment(models.Model):
    post = models.ForeignKey(Post, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name="comments")
    text = models.TextField()

# usage
ann = Author.objects.create(name="Ann")
post = Post.objects.create(title="Hi", author=ann)
post.tags.add(Tag.objects.create(name="django"))
print(post.author.name, ann.posts.count())          # Ann 1
print(Post.objects.filter(author__name="Ann", tags__name="django").count())   # 1
print(Author.objects.filter(posts__comments__isnull=True).distinct().count()) # 1
takeaways: ForeignKey = many-to-one, ManyToManyField = many-to-many, OneToOneField = one-to-one
on_delete decides what deleting the parent does (CASCADE, PROTECT, SET_NULL...)
related_name names the backward link; __ follows links in queries
pitfalls: SET_NULL without null=True on the field, which Django's startup checks reject.

quiz.q: Post has author = ForeignKey(Author, related_name="posts", on_delete=PROTECT). What happens when you delete an author with posts?
options: The deletion is refused with ProtectedError
quiz.explain: PROTECT blocks deleting a referenced object, raising ProtectedError.

concepts.name: The Django admin
concepts.summary: Register models in the Django admin and customise its lists, filters, search and edit pages with ModelAdmin.
concepts.why: The admin gives you a ready-made back office for your data with a few lines of code.
concepts.body:
Most sites need private pages where the team can look up and fix data. Django builds them for you: the **admin** (`django.contrib.admin`) generates pages to create, read, update and delete (**CRUD**) rows of every model you register.

Create a login for yourself with `python manage.py createsuperuser`, run the dev server and visit `/admin/`. A **superuser** is an account with every permission.

Register models in the app's `admin.py`. A plain `admin.site.register(Post)` works; a **`ModelAdmin`** class customises the pages:

- `list_display`: columns on the list page, including methods and related fields
- `list_filter`, `search_fields`, `date_hierarchy`: sidebar filters, a search box, drill-down by date
- `list_editable`, `ordering`, `list_per_page`, `list_select_related`
- `prepopulated_fields = {"slug": ["title"]}`: fills the slug as you type the title
- `readonly_fields`, `fields` or `fieldsets`: shape the edit form
- `autocomplete_fields` or `raw_id_fields`: a searchable picker for a foreign key, instead of a drop-down listing every row
- `inlines`: edit related objects (a post's comments) on the parent's page with `TabularInline` or `StackedInline`
- `actions`: functions run on the rows you tick, such as "publish selected"

`search_fields = ["title", "author__name"]` searches across relationships; prefixes like `"^title"` (starts with) or `"=slug"` (exact) change the matching.

Who sees what is controlled by Django's permissions. Only **staff users** (accounts with `is_staff` on) can log in, and each model has view, add, change and delete permissions; staff see only the models they have permission for.

The admin is meant for trusted staff, not as the interface of your public site. When end users need complex workflows, build normal views for them.
concepts.code:
# blog/admin.py
from django.contrib import admin
from .models import Comment, Post

class CommentInline(admin.TabularInline):
    model = Comment
    extra = 0

@admin.register(Post)
class PostAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    list_display = ["title", "author", "status", "views", "created"]
    list_filter = ["status", "created"]
    search_fields = ["title", "author__name"]
    prepopulated_fields = {"slug": ["title"]}
    autocomplete_fields = ["author"]          # AuthorAdmin needs search_fields
    list_select_related = ["author"]
    date_hierarchy = "created"
    inlines = [CommentInline]
    actions = ["publish"]

    @admin.action(description="Publish selected posts")
    def publish(self, request, queryset):
        updated = queryset.update(status=Post.Status.PUBLISHED)
        self.message_user(request, f"{updated} posts published.")
takeaways: createsuperuser, then register models in admin.py
ModelAdmin options shape lists, search, filters and forms
Inlines edit related rows; actions run on the ticked rows
The admin is for staff, not end users
pitfalls: Using autocomplete_fields without search_fields on the related model's admin, which Django's startup checks reject.

quiz.q: Which ModelAdmin option lets staff edit a post's comments on the post's page?
quiz.explain: Inlines embed forms for related objects within the parent object's change page.

concepts.name: Forms and validation
concepts.summary: Define Form classes, fill them from request.POST, validate with is_valid() and clean methods, and show errors back to the user.
concepts.why: Forms are where data typed by strangers enters your app; Django checks it, converts it and redisplays it with errors for you.
concepts.body:
Anything a visitor types into a form is **untrusted input**: it may be empty, malformed or deliberately malicious. A Django **form class** describes the fields you expect, and Django checks submissions against it; that checking is called **validation**. Each field has a type, a **widget** (which HTML input it is drawn as) and validation rules:

```python
class ContactForm(forms.Form):
    email = forms.EmailField()
    message = forms.CharField(widget=forms.Textarea, max_length=2000)
```

The standard view pattern:

1. `GET`: create an empty, **unbound** form, `ContactForm()`, and render it.
2. `POST`: create a **bound** form from the submitted data, `ContactForm(request.POST)`, and call `form.is_valid()`.
3. If valid, use `form.cleaned_data`: the values converted to Python types (`int`, `date`...). Then redirect, so refreshing the page doesn't submit the form twice.
4. If invalid, render the same bound form again: it remembers what was typed and carries `form.errors`.

Custom validation:

- `clean_<field>(self)` checks one field and returns the cleaned value
- `clean(self)` checks combinations of fields; use `self.add_error("field", "msg")`, or raise `ValidationError` for an error about the whole form
- `validators=[...]` on a field for reusable checks

In templates, `{{ form }}` renders all fields with labels and errors (as `<div>`s by default). For a custom layout, loop over the fields or use `{{ form.email.as_field_group }}` for each one.

Always put `{% csrf_token %}` inside POST forms. Without it, Django refuses the submission with status 403 ("forbidden"). This hidden code blocks **CSRF** (cross-site request forgery): another website secretly making a logged-in visitor's browser submit your form.

Never read `request.POST` directly for your app's logic when a form exists: `cleaned_data` is the checked, typed version. File uploads also need `request.FILES` passed as the second argument and `enctype="multipart/form-data"` on the `<form>` tag.
takeaways: Unbound form for GET, bound form(request.POST) for POST
is_valid() fills cleaned_data or errors
clean_<field>() for one field, clean() for rules across fields
Always include {% csrf_token %} in POST forms
pitfalls: Rendering a fresh empty form after a failed POST, losing the user's input and the error messages.

quiz.q: After form.is_valid() returns True, where should you read the submitted values from?
quiz.explain: cleaned_data contains validated values converted to Python types.

concepts.name: ModelForms
concepts.summary: Generate forms from models with ModelForm, save them to create or update rows, and list fields explicitly.
concepts.why: Most forms edit a row of some model; a ModelForm saves you from describing the same fields twice.
concepts.body:
Most forms edit a model: a "new post" form has the same fields as the `Post` model. A **`ModelForm`** builds its fields from the model, so you don't repeat them:

```python
class PostForm(forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = Post
        fields = ["title", "slug", "body", "tags"]
```

Field types, `max_length`, `choices`, `blank` and help text all come from the model. Validation runs both the form's checks and the model's own (the model method `full_clean()`), including `unique` constraints.

Saving:

- `form.save()` inserts a new row, or updates the object you passed in
- edit an existing object with `PostForm(request.POST, instance=post)`
- `form.save(commit=False)` returns an unsaved object so you can set fields that aren't in the form, like `obj.author = ...`, then call `obj.save()`. Many-to-many links can only be stored once the row exists, so after `commit=False` also call `form.save_m2m()`.

**List fields explicitly.** With `fields = "__all__"` or `exclude = [...]`, any field you add to the model later becomes editable by users automatically. That is a **mass assignment** hole: a user could send `is_staff`, `price` or `owner` along with the form and change it.

Customise with `widgets = {"body": forms.Textarea(attrs={"rows": 10})}`, `labels`, `help_texts`, or by declaring a field yourself on the form class to replace the generated one. Add `clean_<field>` methods as with any other form.

The generic views `CreateView` and `UpdateView` (next lesson) use ModelForms automatically, which is why they need only `model` and `fields` to work.
takeaways: ModelForm derives fields and validation from the model
instance= edits an existing row; save() creates or updates
save(commit=False) lets you set extra fields; then save_m2m()
Always list fields explicitly
pitfalls: Using fields = "__all__", so sensitive fields added to the model later become editable.

quiz.q: You call form.save(commit=False), set obj.author and call obj.save(). The form has a ManyToMany field. What else is needed?
quiz.explain: Many-to-many links need the row to exist first, so after commit=False you must call save_m2m() yourself.

concepts.name: Generic class-based views
concepts.summary: Use ListView, DetailView, CreateView, UpdateView and DeleteView, customize them by overriding methods, and add mixins.
concepts.why: Generic views already implement the common list, detail, create, edit and delete pages, so your code only describes what's different.
concepts.body:
Many views look alike: show a list, show one object, edit it, delete it. **Class-based views** let you reuse that work. They are classes, and `as_view()` turns one into a view your URLconf can use: `path("", PostListView.as_view(), name="list")`.

Django's **generic views** are ready-made classes for the common pages:

- `TemplateView`: just render a template
- `ListView`: a list of objects, split into pages with `paginate_by = 20`; the template gets `object_list` (also as `post_list`) and `page_obj`
- `DetailView`: one object, found by the `pk` or `slug` in the URL; 404 if missing
- `CreateView`, `UpdateView`: a ModelForm; when saved, redirect to `success_url` or to the object's own page (its `get_absolute_url()` method)
- `DeleteView`: ask for confirmation on GET, delete on POST
- `FormView`, `RedirectView`

Each looks for a template named `app/model_suffix.html` by default, such as `blog/post_list.html`, `blog/post_detail.html` and `blog/post_form.html`.

Customise by setting class attributes or overriding methods:

- `get_queryset()`: restrict the objects, for example to the user's own
- `get_context_data(**kwargs)`: add values to the context dict; call `super()` first
- `form_valid(form)`: act before saving, such as setting the author

Extra behaviour comes from **mixins**: `LoginRequiredMixin` (sends visitors who aren't logged in to the login page), `PermissionRequiredMixin`, `UserPassesTestMixin`. Put them **leftmost** in the base classes. Every request first goes through a method called `dispatch`, and the leftmost class's version runs first, so the check happens before any page logic.

Use `reverse_lazy` for `success_url` on the class: the class body runs when the module is imported, before Django has loaded the URLconf, and `reverse_lazy` waits until the URL is actually needed.

Class-based views shine for standard list, detail, create, edit and delete pages; for unusual flows, a function view is often clearer.
takeaways: ListView/DetailView/CreateView/UpdateView/DeleteView cover CRUD
Override get_queryset, get_context_data and form_valid to customize
Mixins like LoginRequiredMixin go leftmost
Use reverse_lazy for class-level URLs
pitfalls: Putting LoginRequiredMixin after the generic view in the bases, so the check doesn't run first.

quiz.q: Why is success_url = reverse_lazy("blog:list") used instead of reverse() on a class attribute?
options: The URLconf isn't loaded when the class body executes at import time
quiz.explain: Class attributes are evaluated when the module is imported, before the URLs are loaded; reverse_lazy waits until the value is used.

concepts.name: Authentication and permissions
concepts.summary: Log users in and out with Django's built-in views, protect views with login_required, and check permissions and groups.
concepts.why: Almost every app needs user accounts, and Django's auth system is secure and complete out of the box.
concepts.body:
Two questions come up on every protected page: who is this visitor (**authentication**, usually by entering a password), and what may they do (**authorization**). `django.contrib.auth` answers both with users, login, permissions and groups.

Passwords are never stored as typed. Django stores a **hash**: a scrambled fingerprint of the password that can be checked but not turned back into it. It uses the PBKDF2 method by default, Argon2 if you configure it. Never store or compare raw passwords yourself.

After a successful log-in, Django remembers the user from request to request with a **session**: a record on the server, linked to the browser by a small value the browser stores and sends back with every request (a **cookie**).

**Login and logout.** Include the built-in views: `path("accounts/", include("django.contrib.auth.urls"))` gives URLs for login, logout, password change and password reset. You supply templates such as `registration/login.html`. The settings `LOGIN_URL`, `LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL` and `LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URL` say where to send people. Log-out requires a POST (a small form with `{% csrf_token %}`), not a link.

In views, `request.user` is the current user, or an `AnonymousUser` for visitors who haven't signed in; check `request.user.is_authenticated`. In templates, `{{ user }}` is available.

**Protecting views:**

- `@login_required` (functions) or `LoginRequiredMixin` (classes) redirect anonymous visitors to `LOGIN_URL?next=...`, so they come back after they log in
- since Django 5.1, adding `LoginRequiredMiddleware` to settings makes every view require login unless marked `@login_not_required`

**Permissions.** Each model gets `add`, `change`, `delete` and `view` permissions automatically, named like `"blog.change_post"`. Check with `user.has_perm("blog.change_post")`, `@permission_required(...)` or `PermissionRequiredMixin`. Give permissions to **user groups** ("Editors") and put users in those groups. Superusers have every permission. For rules about single objects ("only the author may edit"), filter the QuerySet or check ownership in the view.

To log someone in from your own code: `user = authenticate(request, username=..., password=...)`, then `login(request, user)`.
concepts.code:
# mysite/urls.py
from django.urls import include, path
urlpatterns = [path("accounts/", include("django.contrib.auth.urls"))]   # login/, logout/, ...

# settings.py
LOGIN_URL = "login"
LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL = "blog:list"

# blog/views.py
from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required, permission_required
from django.core.exceptions import PermissionDenied
from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404, render

@login_required
def dashboard(request):
    return render(request, "blog/dashboard.html", {"mine": request.user.author.posts.all()})

@permission_required("blog.change_post", raise_exception=True)    # 403 if missing
def moderate(request, pk):
    post = get_object_or_404(Post, pk=pk)
    if not (request.user.is_superuser or post.author.user == request.user):
        raise PermissionDenied
    ...
# templates/registration/login.html:  <form method="post">{% csrf_token %}{{ form }}<button>Log in</button></form>
# logout must be POST: <form method="post" action="{% url 'logout' %}">{% csrf_token %}<button>Log out</button></form>
takeaways: include("django.contrib.auth.urls") gives login, logout and password views
@login_required / LoginRequiredMixin protect views
Permissions are named app_label.action_model and usually given through user groups
Logout is a POST request
pitfalls: Using a plain <a href> for logout; since Django 5.0 LogoutView only accepts POST.

quiz.q: What is the permission codename Django creates for editing Post objects in the blog app?
quiz.explain: Default permissions are add, change, delete and view, named app_label.action_modelname.

concepts.name: Q, F, annotate and aggregate
concepts.summary: Build OR/NOT conditions with Q, refer to columns with F, and compute per-row values and totals with Count, Sum and Avg.
concepts.why: Reports, counters and complex filters run far faster inside the database than in Python loops.
concepts.body:
`filter(a=1, b=2)` can only say AND. **Q objects** wrap single conditions so you can combine them with `|` (OR), `&` (AND) and `~` (NOT):

```python
Post.objects.filter(Q(status="pub") | Q(author__name="Ann"), ~Q(views=0))
```

**F expressions** mean "the value already in this column", so the database can work with it directly:

- compare two columns: `filter(updated__gt=F("created"))`
- update in place: `Post.objects.filter(pk=pk).update(views=F("views") + 1)` runs `views = views + 1` in SQL.

Why does the second one matter? A busy site handles many requests at the same moment. With `post.views += 1; post.save()`, two requests can both read 10 and both write 11, so one visit is never counted. This is a **race condition**, and the result is called a **lost update**. The F version does the read and the write inside the database in one step, so nothing can slip in between.

**`aggregate()`** sums up a whole QuerySet into a dict: `Post.objects.aggregate(total=Sum("views"), avg=Avg("views"))` returns `{"total": 15, "avg": 5.0}`.

**`annotate()`** attaches a computed value to every object:

```python
Author.objects.annotate(n=Count("posts")).filter(n__gte=5).order_by("-n")
```

You can filter and sort by annotations like fields. To count only some related rows, pass a condition: `Count("posts", filter=Q(posts__status="pub"))`.

`values("field").annotate(...)` becomes `GROUP BY field`: `Post.objects.values("author__name").annotate(total=Sum("views"))` adds up the `views` column for each author.

Database functions (`Lower`, `Coalesce`, `TruncMonth`, `Concat`...) and `Case`/`When` (an if/else inside SQL) work anywhere expressions do.

`Exists(...)` and `Subquery(...)` put a whole query inside another, a **subquery**. `OuterRef("pk")` inside it refers to the current row of the outer query, which lets you ask "does this post have an unapproved comment?" in a single SQL statement.

Beware two `Count`s over different many-valued relations in one `annotate()`: the database combines every post with every comment, so both counts come out multiplied. Use `distinct=True` or subqueries.
concepts.code:
from django.db.models import Avg, Count, Exists, F, OuterRef, Q, Sum
from django.db.models.functions import TruncMonth
from blog.models import Author, Comment, Post

popular_or_mine = Post.objects.filter(Q(views__gte=100) | Q(author__name="Ann"), ~Q(status="draft"))

Post.objects.filter(pk=1).update(views=F("views") + 1)       # safe even with simultaneous requests

Post.objects.aggregate(total=Sum("views"), avg=Avg("views"))  # {'total': 15, 'avg': 5.0}

authors = (Author.objects
           .annotate(n_posts=Count("posts"),
                     n_published=Count("posts", filter=Q(posts__status="pub")))
           .filter(n_posts__gte=1)
           .order_by("-n_posts"))
# [(a.name, a.n_posts, a.n_published) for a in authors] -> [('Ann', 2, 1), ('Bo', 1, 1)]

per_author = Post.objects.values("author__name").annotate(total=Sum("views"))  # GROUP BY
per_month = Post.objects.annotate(m=TruncMonth("created")).values("m").annotate(n=Count("id"))

pending = Comment.objects.filter(post=OuterRef("pk"), approved=False)
needs_review = Post.objects.filter(Exists(pending))
takeaways: Q objects build OR/NOT conditions; F refers to a column inside SQL
update(x=F("x") + 1) avoids lost updates from simultaneous requests
aggregate() returns one dict; annotate() adds a value to each object
values(...).annotate(...) is GROUP BY
pitfalls: Incrementing counters in Python with obj.x += 1; obj.save(), which loses updates when requests run at the same time.

quiz.q: What does Author.objects.annotate(n=Count("posts")) return?
options: A dict with the total number of posts
Authors, each with an extra attribute n holding their post count
quiz.explain: annotate adds a computed field per object; aggregate would return a single dict.

concepts.name: Avoiding N+1 queries
concepts.summary: Load related objects efficiently with select_related and prefetch_related, and catch query explosions in tests.
concepts.why: The N+1 query problem is the most common Django performance bug, and it hides in innocent-looking templates.
concepts.body:
Following a relationship on each object of a list runs one query per object. Listing 50 posts with `{{ post.author.name }}` runs 1 query for the posts plus **50** for their authors. This is the **N+1 query** problem: each query is fast, but the trips back and forth to the database add up.

Two tools fix it:

- **`select_related("author")`** follows ForeignKey and OneToOne links with a SQL **JOIN** (one query that combines matching rows of two tables), so posts and authors arrive together. It can go further: `select_related("author__user")`.
- **`prefetch_related("tags", "comments")`** handles many-to-many links and the backward side of a foreign key (an author's posts). It runs one extra query per relation (`WHERE post_id IN (...)`) and matches the results up in Python.

`Prefetch("comments", queryset=Comment.objects.filter(approved=True), to_attr="approved_comments")` chooses what is prefetched and stores it as a list attribute.

A prefetched relation is used only if you access it with `.all()`. Calling `.filter()` on it afterwards runs a new query, so put the filter in a `Prefetch` instead.

Related tools:

- `only("title", "slug")` and `defer("body")` skip loading heavy columns
- `.iterator()` fetches a huge result in chunks instead of holding every object at once
- `bulk_create` and `bulk_update` write many rows in a few queries
- `count()` and `exists()` beat `len(qs)` and `if qs:` when you don't need the objects

**Detect** problems with the `django-debug-toolbar` package during development (it lists every query a page ran) and with `self.assertNumQueries(n)` in tests, which fails when a change sneaks in extra queries. Put `select_related`/`prefetch_related` in the view's QuerySet, not scattered through templates.
concepts.code:
from django.db.models import Prefetch
from blog.models import Comment, Post

# N+1: 1 query for posts + 1 per post for its author
for post in Post.objects.all():
    print(post.author.name)

# 3 queries total: posts JOIN authors, then tags, then approved comments
posts = (Post.objects
         .select_related("author")
         .prefetch_related("tags",
                           Prefetch("comments",
                                    queryset=Comment.objects.filter(approved=True),
                                    to_attr="approved_comments")))
for post in posts:
    print(post.author.name, [t.name for t in post.tags.all()], len(post.approved_comments))

# In tests:
# with self.assertNumQueries(3):
#     self.client.get(reverse("blog:list"))
takeaways: select_related = JOIN for ForeignKey/OneToOne
prefetch_related = one extra query per many-valued relation
Prefetch(queryset=..., to_attr=...) customises prefetching
assertNumQueries catches extra queries creeping back in
pitfalls: Calling .filter() on a prefetched relation, which ignores the prefetched objects and queries again.

quiz.q: Which method should you use to load each post's tags (a ManyToManyField) efficiently?
quiz.explain: select_related only works for single-valued relations; many-to-many needs prefetch_related.

concepts.name: Managers, QuerySet methods and Meta
concepts.summary: Add reusable query methods with custom QuerySets and managers, and declare indexes and constraints in Meta.
concepts.why: Named query methods keep rules like "what counts as published" in one place instead of copied filters everywhere.
concepts.body:
When the same filter appears in many views, give it a name. Write the method on a **custom QuerySet** (your own subclass of `models.QuerySet`) and use it as the model's manager:

```python
class PostQuerySet(models.QuerySet):
    def published(self):
        return self.filter(status="pub")

class Post(models.Model):
    objects = PostQuerySet.as_manager()
```

Now `Post.objects.published().filter(author=a)` reads naturally. Because the method lives on the QuerySet, it can be used anywhere in a chain, `Post.objects.filter(author=a).published()` too; a method only on the manager would work only at the start.

**Model methods** hold behaviour of a single row: `get_absolute_url()` (the object's own page, used by the admin and generic views), values computed from fields (often with `@property`, so they read like attributes), and actions like `publish()`. A good rule: logic about many rows goes on the QuerySet, logic about one row on the model.

`Meta` options worth knowing:

- `ordering`: the default sort, applied to every query, so keep it cheap and backed by an index
- `indexes = [models.Index(fields=["status", "-created"])]`
- `constraints`: `UniqueConstraint(fields=["author", "slug"], name="...")` and `CheckConstraint(condition=Q(views__gte=0), name="...")`, enforced by the database and by `full_clean()`
- `verbose_name`, `verbose_name_plural`, `db_table`, `get_latest_by`

Database constraints beat checks in Python: they hold even for `update()` calls, admin edits and other programs writing to the same database.

Note that `save()` does not call `full_clean()`; validation runs in ModelForms or when you call it yourself.
takeaways: Put reusable filters on a QuerySet subclass; expose it with as_manager()
Single-row behaviour and get_absolute_url() go on the model
Declare indexes and constraints in Meta; the database enforces them
pitfalls: Expecting model.save() to run field validation; it doesn't call full_clean().

quiz.q: Why define published() on a QuerySet subclass rather than only on a Manager?
options: So it can be chained after other filters, e.g. Post.objects.filter(...).published()
quiz.explain: QuerySet methods are available on every QuerySet in a chain, not just at the start.

concepts.name: Settings and environments
concepts.summary: Organise settings.py for development and production, read secrets from environment variables, and access settings the safe way.
concepts.why: Wrong settings cause most failed deployments and security incidents in Django apps.
concepts.body:
`settings.py` is a plain Python module. Django finds it through `DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE`, an **environment variable**: a named value the operating system hands to a program when it starts, outside the code. `manage.py`, `wsgi.py` and `asgi.py` set a default for it. Key settings:

- `DEBUG`: shows detailed error pages, including your code and settings, to anyone; must be `False` in production
- `SECRET_KEY`: a long random value Django uses to sign data it hands out, such as the value that keeps a browser signed in and password-reset links, so forgeries are spotted. Keep it secret and don't change it casually.
- `ALLOWED_HOSTS`: the site names it answers to, such as `example.com`; required when `DEBUG = False`
- `DATABASES`, `CACHES`, `INSTALLED_APPS`, `MIDDLEWARE`, `TEMPLATES`, `STORAGES`
- `TIME_ZONE` and `USE_TZ = True` (the default): store dates and times in UTC

A **secret** is anything like a password or key that must not leak. Keep secrets, and values that differ between your computer and production, out of the code you commit to version control. The simplest robust approach reads them from environment variables:

```python
SECRET_KEY = os.environ["DJANGO_SECRET_KEY"]       # crash early if missing
DEBUG = os.environ.get("DJANGO_DEBUG", "") == "1"
```

Libraries like `django-environ` add helpers for reading booleans, lists and database URLs. Some teams split settings into modules (`settings/base.py`, `dev.py`, `prod.py`) that import from a shared base; either way, the defaults should be the safe production values.

In code, always read settings with `from django.conf import settings`, never by importing your settings module. That way the active module is used and tests can change values with `@override_settings`.

`python manage.py diffsettings` shows what differs from Django's defaults, and `python manage.py check --deploy` lists insecure production settings.
concepts.code:
# mysite/settings.py (excerpt)
import os
from pathlib import Path

BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
SECRET_KEY = os.environ["DJANGO_SECRET_KEY"]                 # required
DEBUG = os.environ.get("DJANGO_DEBUG", "0") == "1"           # safe default: off
ALLOWED_HOSTS = os.environ.get("DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS", "localhost").split(",")

DATABASES = {
    "default": {
        "ENGINE": "django.db.backends.postgresql",
        "NAME": os.environ.get("POSTGRES_DB", "blog"),
        "USER": os.environ.get("POSTGRES_USER", "blog"),
        "PASSWORD": os.environ.get("POSTGRES_PASSWORD", ""),
        "HOST": os.environ.get("POSTGRES_HOST", "localhost"),
        "CONN_MAX_AGE": 60,                                  # reuse connections
    }
}

# anywhere else in the code:
from django.conf import settings
page_size = getattr(settings, "BLOG_PAGE_SIZE", 20)
takeaways: `DEBUG` off, a secret `SECRET_KEY` and `ALLOWED_HOSTS` are required in production
Read secrets and per-machine values from environment variables
Access settings via django.conf.settings
check --deploy finds insecure production settings
pitfalls: Committing SECRET_KEY and DEBUG = True to version control and deploying them.

quiz.q: Why import settings with from django.conf import settings rather than import mysite.settings?
options: It uses the active DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE and respects overrides like @override_settings
quiz.explain: django.conf.settings always points at whichever settings module is active, including values changed by tests.

concepts.name: Testing Django apps
concepts.summary: Write tests with django.test.TestCase, the test client and setUpTestData, and check responses, templates and query counts.
concepts.why: Django apps change constantly, and its test tools make full request-to-database tests fast and independent of each other.
concepts.body:
`python manage.py test` finds tests in files named `test*.py`, creates a separate, empty **test database**, runs the tests and deletes it afterwards. Your real data is never touched.

Choose a base class:

- `SimpleTestCase`: no database access
- **`TestCase`**: runs each test inside a transaction and rolls it back at the end, so no test sees another's changes, and it's fast. The usual choice.
- `TransactionTestCase`: really commits, for testing code that depends on commits themselves
- `LiveServerTestCase`: starts a real server, so tools like Playwright or Selenium can drive a real browser against your site

`setUpTestData(cls)` creates data once per class, much faster than `setUp`, which runs before every test. Each test still sees the data fresh, thanks to the rollback.

`self.client` is a **test client**: a pretend browser that sends requests through your whole app (URLs, views, templates, database) without starting a server:

- `self.client.get(reverse("blog:list"), {"q": "x"})`, `.post(url, data)`
- `self.client.force_login(user)` signs a user in without the login form
- checks: `assertEqual(resp.status_code, 200)`, `assertContains(resp, "Hello")`, `assertRedirects`, `assertTemplateUsed`, `assertFormError`
- `resp.context["posts"]` gives the values the view passed to the template

`self.assertNumQueries(n)` fails if a change makes a page run more queries (an N+1 creeping back in). `@override_settings(...)` changes settings for one test. `RequestFactory` builds a request object so a unit test can call a view directly.

Many teams use **pytest-django**, which runs the same Django machinery with pytest fixtures and plain `assert`.
concepts.code:
from django.contrib.auth.models import User
from django.test import TestCase
from django.urls import reverse
from blog.models import Author, Post

class PostViewsTests(TestCase):
    @classmethod
    def setUpTestData(cls):                       # runs once per class
        cls.user = User.objects.create_user("ann", password="pw")
        cls.author = Author.objects.create(name="Ann", user=cls.user)
        Post.objects.create(title="Hello", slug="hello", author=cls.author, status="pub")

    def test_list_shows_published_posts(self):
        with self.assertNumQueries(2):            # count + page (author via select_related)
            resp = self.client.get(reverse("blog:list"))
        self.assertContains(resp, "Hello")
        self.assertTemplateUsed(resp, "blog/post_list.html")
    def test_create_requires_login(self):
        resp = self.client.get(reverse("blog:create"))
        self.assertRedirects(resp, f"{reverse('login')}?next={reverse('blog:create')}")
    def test_logged_in_user_can_create(self):
        self.client.force_login(self.user)
        resp = self.client.post(reverse("blog:create"), {"title": "New", "slug": "new", "body": "x"})
        self.assertEqual(resp.status_code, 302)
        self.assertTrue(Post.objects.filter(slug="new", author=self.author).exists())
takeaways: TestCase isolates each test in a rolled-back transaction
setUpTestData creates shared data once per class
self.client runs requests through the whole app; force_login skips the login form
assertNumQueries catches extra queries
pitfalls: Creating heavy fixtures in setUp for every test instead of setUpTestData.

quiz.q: How does django.test.TestCase keep tests from affecting each other's data?
options: It deletes all rows after each test
It wraps each test in a transaction and rolls it back
It creates a new database per test
quiz.explain: Each test runs inside a transaction that is rolled back at the end, so its changes disappear.

concepts.name: Transactions and concurrency
concepts.summary: Group writes with transaction.atomic, run side effects with on_commit, and lock rows with select_for_update.
concepts.why: Multi-step writes and simultaneous requests corrupt data unless you control transactions and locking.
concepts.body:
By default Django commits every query as soon as it runs, which databases call **autocommit**. When several writes must succeed or fail together as one **atomic** step, such as taking money from one account and adding it to another, wrap them in **`transaction.atomic()`**, used as a decorator or a `with` block. If an exception escapes the block, everything in it is rolled back.

An `atomic` block inside another creates a **savepoint**: a bookmark inside the transaction. If the inner block fails, only its work is undone and the outer one can carry on, provided you catch the exception **outside** the inner block. Catching a database error inside an atomic block and continuing is wrong: the transaction is broken, and the next query raises `TransactionManagementError`.

`ATOMIC_REQUESTS = True` in a database's settings wraps every view in a transaction. It's simple, but keeps a transaction open for the whole request; explicit `atomic` blocks are more precise.

**Side effects after commit.** Sending an email or handing a job to a background **worker** (a separate process that runs queued jobs) from inside a transaction is risky. The transaction may roll back after the email has gone, or the worker may start before the data is committed and not find it. `transaction.on_commit(callback)` runs the callback only after a successful commit and drops it on rollback.

**Simultaneous requests.** Two requests that read and then write the same row can overwrite each other. Options:

- `F()` expressions for arithmetic updates
- `select_for_update()` inside `atomic` places a **lock** on the selected rows until commit, so other requests wait. `nowait=True` fails at once instead of waiting; `skip_locked=True` skips locked rows, handy when several workers take jobs from one table.
- optimistic locking: keep a `version` column and update with `filter(pk=..., version=v).update(..., version=v + 1)`; if 0 rows changed, someone else got there first
- unique constraints, catching the `IntegrityError` the database raises when two requests insert the same value

When two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, both wait forever, a **deadlock**; the database then kills one. Lock rows in a consistent order (for example by `pk`) to avoid it. Keep transactions short, and never wait on slow calls to other services while holding locks.
concepts.code:
from django.db import IntegrityError, transaction
from django.db.models import F
from shop.models import Account, Order, Transfer
from shop.tasks import send_receipt
@transaction.atomic
def transfer(from_id, to_id, amount):
    # lock both rows in a consistent order to avoid deadlocks
    accounts = {a.pk: a for a in Account.objects.select_for_update().filter(pk__in=[from_id, to_id]).order_by("pk")}
    if accounts[from_id].balance < amount:
        raise ValueError("insufficient funds")            # rolls everything back
    Account.objects.filter(pk=from_id).update(balance=F("balance") - amount)
    Account.objects.filter(pk=to_id).update(balance=F("balance") + amount)
    t = Transfer.objects.create(source_id=from_id, target_id=to_id, amount=amount)
    transaction.on_commit(lambda: send_receipt.enqueue(t.pk))   # only after COMMIT
    return t
def place_order(user, cart):
    with transaction.atomic():
        order = Order.objects.create(user=user)
        try:
            with transaction.atomic():                  # savepoint
                order.apply_coupon(cart.coupon)
        except IntegrityError:
            order.note = "coupon already used"         # outer transaction still fine
        order.save()
    return order
takeaways: atomic() makes a block all-or-nothing; nesting creates savepoints
Catch database errors outside the atomic block that failed
on_commit runs side effects only after a successful commit
select_for_update locks rows until the transaction ends
pitfalls: Sending emails or enqueuing jobs inside a transaction that might roll back.

quiz.q: Inside an atomic block you create an order and enqueue a job that reads it. Why use transaction.on_commit?
options: Jobs can't be enqueued inside atomic
The worker might run before the commit and not see the order (or the transaction might roll back)
quiz.explain: on_commit waits until the data is committed, and drops the callback if the transaction rolls back.

concepts.name: Middleware
concepts.summary: Write middleware that wraps every request and response, get the order right, and use the process_view and process_exception hooks.
concepts.why: Jobs that apply to every request, like timing, extra headers or request IDs, belong in middleware rather than in every view.
concepts.body:
Some jobs apply to every request: measuring how long it took, adding a header to every response, checking the session. Rather than repeating them in each view, Django runs **middleware**: a chain of wrappers around your views. Each middleware is a function that receives `get_response` (the next layer inward) and returns a function that handles one request:

```python
def timing_middleware(get_response):
    # one-time setup when the server starts
    def middleware(request):
        # before the view
        response = get_response(request)
        # after the view
        return response
    return middleware
```

Classes work the same way, with `__init__(self, get_response)` and `__call__(self, request)`.

List middleware in `settings.MIDDLEWARE`. **Order matters**: requests pass through top to bottom, responses come back bottom to top, like the layers of an onion. `AuthenticationMiddleware` needs `SessionMiddleware` above it, and `SecurityMiddleware` usually comes first.

A middleware can answer by itself, returning a response without calling `get_response`, for example a maintenance page or turning away a visitor's IP address. The inner layers and the view then never run.

Optional methods on class-based middleware:

- `process_view(request, view_func, view_args, view_kwargs)`: after Django has matched the URL to a view, before the view runs
- `process_exception(request, exception)`: when the view raises; return a response to handle it
- `process_template_response(request, response)`: change a `TemplateResponse` before it is rendered

Built-in middleware handles sessions, logins, CSRF checks, one-time messages, headers that stop other sites from showing your pages inside a frame, compression, the visitor's language, and (in Django 6.0) Content Security Policy, a header listing where a page may load scripts from.

Middleware runs on every request, so keep it fast. If you use async views (a later lesson), mark middleware `async_capable` and give it an async path too, so Django doesn't have to switch between the two styles on every request.
concepts.code:
# core/middleware.py
import logging, time, uuid

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
class RequestIdMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response               # called once at startup
    def __call__(self, request):
        request.id = request.headers.get("X-Request-ID") or uuid.uuid4().hex
        start = time.perf_counter()
        response = self.get_response(request)          # inner middleware + view
        response["X-Request-ID"] = request.id
        log.info("%s %s %s %.1fms", request.id, request.path, response.status_code,
                 (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000)
        return response
