    def process_exception(self, request, exception):
        log.exception("request %s failed", request.id)
        return None                                    # let Django's handling continue
# settings.py
MIDDLEWARE = [
    "django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware",
    "core.middleware.RequestIdMiddleware",
    "django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware",
    # ... CommonMiddleware, CsrfViewMiddleware, AuthenticationMiddleware, ...
]
takeaways: Middleware wraps get_response: code before it runs on the request, code after it on the response
MIDDLEWARE order: top-down for requests, bottom-up for responses
Returning early skips the inner layers and the view
process_view / process_exception hooks give finer control
pitfalls: Placing a middleware that uses request.user above AuthenticationMiddleware.

quiz.q: Middleware A is listed above B in MIDDLEWARE. In which order do they see the response?
quiz.explain: Responses travel back up the list, so the inner middleware (B) handles them before the outer one (A).

concepts.name: Signals
concepts.summary: React to model and login events with post_save and friends, connect receivers in AppConfig.ready(), and know when to avoid them.
concepts.why: Signals let apps react to each other without importing each other, but used carelessly they hide what code runs when.
concepts.body:
Sometimes one app should react when something happens in another: create a profile whenever a user is saved, say. **Signals** are Django's announcements; any function can subscribe to one. Common built-ins:

- models: `pre_save`, `post_save` (with a `created` flag), `pre_delete`, `post_delete`, `m2m_changed`
- requests: `request_started`, `request_finished`
- auth: `user_logged_in`, `user_logged_out`, `user_login_failed`

A subscribing function is a **receiver**. Connect it with the `@receiver` decorator, naming the model whose events you want as `sender`:

```python
@receiver(post_save, sender=User)
def create_profile(sender, instance, created, **kwargs): ...
```

Receivers must accept `**kwargs`. Put them in `signals.py` and import that module in the `ready()` method of your app's `AppConfig` (the class in `apps.py`, run once at startup). Otherwise the module may never be imported and the receiver never connected. Pass `dispatch_uid="..."` if a module might be imported twice, so the receiver isn't connected twice.

You can define your own: `order_paid = Signal()` and `order_paid.send(sender=Order, order=o)`.

Know the limits:

- `QuerySet.update()`, `bulk_create()` and `bulk_update()` don't send `pre_save`/`post_save`
- receivers run **synchronously**: right away, one after another, inside the same transaction. A slow receiver slows the request, and an exception in one breaks the save.
- the code that saves gives no hint that receivers exist, which makes the program harder to follow and test

Good uses: letting a reusable app react to another app's events without importing it, clearing cached data when a row changes, and writing an **audit log** (a permanent record of who changed what, and when). If both sides are your own code, a plain function call (`create_user_with_profile()`) or a model method is usually clearer.
takeaways: @receiver(signal, sender=Model) connects a function to an event
Import signal modules in AppConfig.ready()
update() and bulk operations don't send save signals
Prefer plain function calls when both sides are your code
pitfalls: Relying on post_save for logic that must also run after queryset.update() or bulk_create().

quiz.q: Which operation does NOT run post_save receivers?
quiz.explain: QuerySet.update() runs a single SQL UPDATE without loading instances, so no save signals are sent.

concepts.name: Custom user models
concepts.summary: Start projects with a custom user model, reference it via AUTH_USER_MODEL and get_user_model, and add email login.
concepts.why: Changing the user model after the first migration is painful, so it's a day-one decision.
concepts.body:
Every project has users, and many tables end up with a foreign key to the user table. That's why Django's docs recommend that **every new project** define its own user model from the start, even an empty one. Switching later means rewriting migrations and foreign keys across all your apps.

The easy version extends `AbstractUser`, keeping username, password, permissions and the admin integration:

```python
class User(AbstractUser):
    pass
```

and in settings: `AUTH_USER_MODEL = "accounts.User"`, set **before** the first `migrate`.

To log in with email instead of a username, either keep `AbstractUser` and set `USERNAME_FIELD = "email"` with a unique email field and `REQUIRED_FIELDS = []` (also removing the username field), or build on `AbstractBaseUser` and `PermissionsMixin`. Either way you need a custom manager whose `create_user` and `create_superuser` methods take an email instead of a username (see the code).

Referencing the user model correctly:

- in model fields: `models.ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, ...)`
- in other code: `get_user_model()` returns whichever class is configured
- never `from django.contrib.auth.models import User` in reusable code

Register it in the admin with `admin.site.register(User, UserAdmin)` (or a `UserAdmin` subclass that shows your fields).

For extra per-user data that signing in doesn't need, such as a bio or preferences, a separate `Profile` model with a `OneToOneField` to the user keeps the user table small, and can be added at any time.
takeaways: Define a custom user model at project start; set AUTH_USER_MODEL before the first migration
Extend AbstractUser for the easy path
Reference users via settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL and get_user_model()
pitfalls: Importing django.contrib.auth.models.User directly in apps, which breaks with a custom user model.

quiz.q: How should a ForeignKey to the user be declared in a reusable app?
quiz.explain: settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL resolves to whichever user model the project configured.

concepts.name: Security features and hardening
concepts.summary: Use Django's protections against CSRF, XSS, SQL injection and clickjacking, and turn on HTTPS settings and a Content Security Policy.
concepts.why: Django is secure by default only if you keep its protections on and set the production settings correctly.
concepts.body:
Django defends against the classic web attacks, as long as you don't switch the defences off:

- **SQL injection**: the ORM sends values separately from the SQL. With `raw()` or `cursor.execute()`, pass values in the `params` list, never with f-strings.
- **XSS** (cross-site scripting: getting the attacker's JavaScript to run in other visitors' browsers): templates autoescape. `|safe`, `mark_safe` and `{% autoescape off %}` turn that off; to build HTML in Python, use `format_html()`, which escapes its arguments.
- **CSRF**: `CsrfViewMiddleware` demands the hidden token on every POST (and other requests that change data). Include `{% csrf_token %}` in forms, and send it in the `X-CSRFToken` header from JavaScript. Avoid `@csrf_exempt` except for URLs that check identity some other way, such as an API key.
- **Clickjacking** (another site showing your page in an invisible frame to trick clicks): `XFrameOptionsMiddleware` sends `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, which forbids framing.
- Fake domain names in requests: `ALLOWED_HOSTS` rejects them.

**HTTPS** is HTTP with encryption, the padlock in the address bar. Settings for production:

- `SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True`: send `http://` visitors to `https://`
- `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True` and `CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True`: cookies travel only over HTTPS
- `SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS` (start small) and `SECURE_HSTS_INCLUDE_SUBDOMAINS`: **HSTS** tells browsers to use only HTTPS for your site from now on
- `SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER = ("HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO", "https")`: needed when a server in front of Django handles the encryption and passes requests on, so Django can tell the original request was secure

**Content Security Policy** (CSP) is built in since Django 6.0. It is a header listing where the page may load scripts and other files from; the browser refuses everything else, which blunts XSS. Add `django.middleware.csp.ContentSecurityPolicyMiddleware` and set `SECURE_CSP` (or `SECURE_CSP_REPORT_ONLY` to only report problems while testing) using constants from `django.utils.csp.CSP`. With `CSP.NONCE` in a rule and `django.template.context_processors.csp` added to the template settings, templates add `nonce="{{ csp_nonce }}"` to inline scripts: a **nonce** is a random value made fresh for each response, so only your own inline scripts carry it.

Also: never run with `DEBUG = True` in production, keep Django updated, use the strongest password hashing you can afford, and run `python manage.py check --deploy` in your automated checks.
concepts.code: # settings.py (production) from django.utils.csp import CSP DEBUG = False ALLOWED_HOSTS = ["blog.example.com"] SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER = ("HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO", "https") SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS = 3600 # raise to a year once verified MIDDLEWARE.insert(1, "django.middleware.csp.ContentSecurityPolicyMiddleware") SECURE_CSP = { "default-src": [CSP.SELF], "script-src": [CSP.SELF, CSP.NONCE], "img-src": [CSP.SELF, "https:"], } TEMPLATES[0]["OPTIONS"]["context_processors"].append("django.template.context_processors.csp") # Safe raw SQL and HTML building from django.db import connection from django.utils.html import format_html def search(term): with connection.cursor() as cur: cur.execute("SELECT id FROM blog_post WHERE title LIKE %s", [f"%{term}%"]) # params! return cur.fetchall() link = format_html('{}', "/u/1", "
takeaways: ORM and params prevent SQL injection; never build SQL with string formatting
Autoescaping, CSRF tokens and X-Frame-Options are on by default; don't bypass them
Turn on HTTPS redirects, secure cookies and HSTS in production
Django 6.0 has a built-in Content Security Policy via middleware and SECURE_CSP
pitfalls: Marking user content with mark_safe or |safe to "fix" escaped HTML, which reopens the door to XSS.

quiz.q: Which raw query is safe from SQL injection?
options: cur.execute("SELECT * FROM t WHERE name = '%s'" % name)
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM t WHERE name = " + name)
quiz.explain: Passing values as parameters lets the database driver handle them as data; string formatting pastes them into the SQL.

concepts.name: Caching
concepts.summary: Configure a cache backend such as Redis and cache data, views and template fragments, with a plan for keeping it up to date.
concepts.why: Caching is often the cheapest way to make a slow page fast, provided you keep it correct.
concepts.body:
If a page spends a second computing the same top-10 list for every visitor, compute it once and keep the result for a while. Keeping results for reuse is called a **cache**. Each value is stored under a name, its key, and usually given a **timeout** after which it expires.

Choose where cached values live, the **cache backend**, in the `CACHES` setting:

- `LocMemCache` (the default): inside each server process's own memory; fine for development only
- `RedisCache` and `PyMemcacheCache`: a separate service shared by all processes and servers. **Redis** is a fast in-memory database often used for this.
- `DatabaseCache` and `FileBasedCache`

Caching levels, from finest to coarsest:

- **Low-level**: `from django.core.cache import cache`, then `cache.get(key)`, `cache.set(key, value, timeout=300)`, `cache.get_or_set(key, callable, timeout)`, `cache.delete(key)`, `cache.incr(key)`. Use it for expensive values, such as aggregates or results fetched from other services.
- **Template fragments**: `{% load cache %}{% cache 600 sidebar request.user.pk %}...{% endcache %}` caches part of a page, with a separate copy for each value of the extra arguments.
- **Per view**: `@cache_page(60 * 15)` caches whole responses, keyed by URL. If the page differs per signed-in user or language, add `@vary_on_cookie` or similar, or don't cache it this way.
- **Per site**: `UpdateCacheMiddleware` and `FetchFromCacheMiddleware`, rarely right beyond simple public sites.

Keeping the cache correct when data changes, **cache invalidation**, is the hard part. Strategies:

- short timeouts, when slightly old data is acceptable
- delete or update keys when data changes, in the code that writes or in signals
- versioned keys: include `updated_at` or a version number in the key, so new data naturally uses a new key

Browsers and CDNs cache too. Django can send the headers that steer them: `ETag`/`Last-Modified` (via `@condition` or `ConditionalGetMiddleware`) let a browser ask "has this changed?" and get a tiny "no" back, and `Cache-Control` says how long a copy may be reused.

`functools.cached_property` on a model remembers a value on that one object only, not across requests.
takeaways: Use a shared cache backend like Redis in production; LocMemCache is separate in every process
Low-level cache functions for data, {% cache %} for fragments, @cache_page for whole views
Plan invalidation: timeouts, explicit deletes or versioned keys
pitfalls: Using @cache_page on a page with user-specific content, serving one user's page to others.

quiz.q: Your site runs as 4 separate server processes. Why is LocMemCache a poor choice?
options: Each worker process has its own separate cache, so data is duplicated and invalidation is inconsistent
quiz.explain: LocMemCache lives inside each process, so the processes don't share entries or deletions.

concepts.name: Background tasks
concepts.summary: Define tasks with Django 6.0's @task decorator, queue them with enqueue(), and choose a backend or a library like Celery to run them.
concepts.why: Slow work such as emails, exports and calls to other services must happen outside the request, or pages get slow.
concepts.body:
A visitor waits for every millisecond your view spends. Slow or unreliable work, such as sending email, generating a report or notifying another service, should run later, outside the request. That is a **background task**: the view puts a note in a queue and returns at once, and a worker process picks the note up and does the job.

Django 6.0 adds a built-in **Tasks framework** (`django.tasks`) that standardises how you define and queue such work:

```python
@task
def send_welcome_email(user_id): ...

send_welcome_email.enqueue(user.pk)
```

`enqueue()` returns a `TaskResult` with an `id` and `status`; `get_result(id)` looks it up later. Options such as `priority`, `queue_name` and `run_after` can be set on the decorator or with `.using(...)`.

The **backend**, the code that actually stores and runs queued tasks, is set in the `TASKS` setting. Django ships only two:

- `ImmediateBackend` (the default): runs the task **synchronously**, right away inside the `enqueue()` call; convenient in development
- `DummyBackend`: stores results without running anything, useful in tests

Django does **not** include a worker. For real background work you need a backend from a separate package (such as `django-tasks`, the reference version with a database backend and a worker command), or you keep using an established library such as **Celery** or **RQ**, with its own decorator and workers.

Rules that apply to any task system:

- pass IDs, not model objects: arguments must be stored as JSON (for `django.tasks`), and the row may change before the task runs
- queue tasks after the commit: `transaction.on_commit(lambda: task.enqueue(order.pk))`
- make tasks **idempotent**, safe to run twice with the same result, because a failed task may be retried and duplicates happen
- define tasks as top-level functions in a module, so workers can import them
concepts.code:
# settings.py
TASKS = {"default": {"BACKEND": "django.tasks.backends.immediate.ImmediateBackend"}}
# production: a worker-based backend from a third-party package

# accounts/tasks.py
from django.core.mail import send_mail
from django.tasks import task

@task(priority=10)
def send_welcome_email(user_id):
    from accounts.models import User
    user = User.objects.get(pk=user_id)          # fetch fresh data in the task
    send_mail("Welcome!", f"Hi {user.first_name}", None, [user.email])
    return user.email

# accounts/views.py
from django.db import transaction

def signup_done(user):
    transaction.on_commit(lambda: send_welcome_email.enqueue(user.pk))

# shell
result = send_welcome_email.enqueue(1)
print(result.status, result.return_value)        # SUCCESSFUL ann@example.com  (ImmediateBackend)
takeaways: Django 6.0: @task defines a task, .enqueue() queues it
Built-in backends: ImmediateBackend (runs at once) and DummyBackend (tests); real workers come from separate packages
Pass IDs, enqueue on commit, make tasks idempotent
pitfalls: Passing model objects or other values that can't be turned into JSON as task arguments.

quiz.q: With the default ImmediateBackend, when does an enqueued task run?
quiz.explain: ImmediateBackend runs the task right away inside enqueue(); real background work needs a worker-based backend.

concepts.name: Deploying Django
concepts.summary: Run Django under Gunicorn or Uvicorn behind a reverse proxy, run collectstatic and migrations on release, and set up databases and logs.
concepts.why: Getting from runserver to a reliable production service follows a well-known checklist.
concepts.body:
`runserver` handles one developer. A live site needs a production setup, usually made of these parts.

**App server.** Django speaks **WSGI**, the standard way a Python web app and a server talk: the server calls your app once per request. **Gunicorn** is the usual WSGI server: `gunicorn mysite.wsgi` starts several worker processes so requests are handled in parallel. For async views and WebSockets (connections that stay open for live updates), Django also speaks **ASGI**, served by **Uvicorn**: `uvicorn mysite.asgi:application`, or `gunicorn -k uvicorn_worker.UvicornWorker mysite.asgi`.

**Reverse proxy.** A server such as Nginx sits in front of the app server and receives every request first. It handles HTTPS encryption, absorbs slow clients so your workers don't wait on them, and can send static files itself. With several app servers, a **load balancer** spreads requests across them.

**Database.** Usually PostgreSQL. Opening a connection is slow, so reuse them: `CONN_MAX_AGE` keeps each connection open between requests (add `CONN_HEALTH_CHECKS = True`), and on PostgreSQL Django 5.1+ can use psycopg's built-in **connection pool**, a set of open connections shared by requests.

**Files.** Static files come from `collectstatic`, sent by WhiteNoise, the proxy or a CDN. User uploads go to **object storage** (online file storage like Amazon S3) via `django-storages`.

Release steps, in order: build the release package (often a container image: a sealed package of the app and everything it needs, built from a recipe like the code), run `collectstatic --noinput`, run `migrate` once as its own step, then start the new app processes.

Configuration checklist (`python manage.py check --deploy` covers much of it):

- `DEBUG = False`, a real `SECRET_KEY`, `ALLOWED_HOSTS`, and `CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS` if forms are posted from another of your domains
- HTTPS settings and `SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER` behind the proxy
- `LOGGING` writing to the terminal output, which the hosting platform collects, plus an error tracker such as Sentry
- the cache on Redis; sessions in the database or the cache
- a **health check** URL that touches the database, so the platform can spot and restart a broken copy

During a release, old and new code run side by side for a while. Write migrations that the old code still works with (**backward compatible**), for example add a column before the code that needs it.
concepts.code:
# Dockerfile (excerpt): a recipe for the container image that runs the site
FROM python:3.13-slim
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=mysite.settings
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN DJANGO_SECRET_KEY=build-only python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
RUN useradd --create-home app                  # don't run as the all-powerful root user
USER app
CMD ["gunicorn", "mysite.wsgi", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3", "--access-logfile", "-"]

# release step (run once per deploy, before switching traffic):
#   python manage.py migrate --noinput
# automated checks before merging:
#   python manage.py check --deploy --fail-level WARNING
takeaways: Gunicorn (WSGI) or Uvicorn (ASGI) behind a reverse proxy
collectstatic when building, migrate as a separate release step
check --deploy, reused database connections, logs to the terminal output
Keep migrations compatible with the previous code version
pitfalls: Running migrations automatically in every app process at startup, so several copies change the database at once.

quiz.q: Why run manage.py migrate as a separate release step rather than in every app copy's startup command?
options: migrate is too slow for startup
Several copies would run it at the same time and collide, and a failure would keep crashing every copy
quiz.explain: One ordered migration step avoids simultaneous schema changes and keeps app startup simple.

concepts.name: How QuerySets work
concepts.summary: Understand QuerySet laziness, cloning, the result cache, how SQL is generated, and the multi-valued filter() gotcha.
concepts.why: Expert ORM use means predicting exactly which SQL runs, and when.
concepts.body:
A QuerySet is a thin wrapper around a **`Query`** object: a tree of Python objects describing the tables, joins, WHERE conditions, annotations and ordering. Each chained method (`filter`, `annotate`, `order_by`) **clones** the QuerySet and changes the copy's query. So a QuerySet never changes under you, and it's safe to reuse one as a base for others.

When the results are needed, the `Query` is handed to a **SQLCompiler** belonging to the database backend (the part of Django written for PostgreSQL, SQLite and so on), which turns the tree into SQL text plus parameters. `str(qs.query)` shows an approximation (the parameters are not properly quoted), and `qs.explain()` asks the database for its **query plan**, the steps it will take to answer.

**Evaluation** happens on iteration, `len()`, `list()`, `bool()`, `repr()`, pickling (Python's way of saving an object as bytes) and slicing with a step. Results are kept in the QuerySet's **result cache**: iterating the same QuerySet twice runs one query, but building a new one (`qs.filter(...)`, `qs.all()`) starts fresh. Indexing a QuerySet that hasn't run yet (`qs[0]`) runs a `LIMIT 1` query each time.

`count()`, `exists()` and `aggregate()` run their own queries unless the cache is already filled (`count()` then just uses `len()` of the cache).

**The multi-valued relationship gotcha:** conditions inside **one** `filter()` call on a relation with many rows (a post's comments) must match the **same** related row; conditions in **separate** `filter()` calls may match **different** rows:

```python
Post.objects.filter(comments__text="spam", comments__approved=True)    # same comment
Post.objects.filter(comments__text="spam").filter(comments__approved=True)  # any comments
```

The second form also adds a second join. With `DEBUG = True`, `connection.queries` lists the SQL that ran; `CaptureQueriesContext` does the same in tests.
concepts.code:
from django.db import connection
from django.test.utils import CaptureQueriesContext
from blog.models import Post

base = Post.objects.filter(status="pub")
recent = base.order_by("-created")        # a clone; base is unchanged

with CaptureQueriesContext(connection) as ctx:
    posts = Post.objects.all()
    list(posts); list(posts)               # 1 query: second pass uses the result cache
    posts.filter(views__gt=0).exists()     # new QuerySet -> new query
    posts.all()[0]                         # new clone -> LIMIT 1 query
print(len(ctx))                            # 3

# Same comment must match both conditions vs. any comments matching each:
same = Post.objects.filter(comments__text="spam", comments__approved=True)
anyc = Post.objects.filter(comments__text="spam").filter(comments__approved=True)
print(same.count(), anyc.count())          # e.g. 1 2

print(str(same.query).count("JOIN"), str(anyc.query).count("JOIN"))   # 1 2
print(base.explain())                      # the database's query plan
takeaways: Chaining clones the QuerySet; each clone holds a Query tree
Evaluated QuerySets cache results; new clones query again
Conditions in one filter() on a multi-valued relation must match the same related row
str(qs.query), explain() and CaptureQueriesContext reveal the SQL
pitfalls: Splitting conditions across filter() calls on a reverse/M2M relation and getting broader results than intended.

quiz.q: posts = Post.objects.all(); list(posts); list(posts). How many queries run?
quiz.explain: The first evaluation fills the result cache, and the second iteration reuses it.

concepts.name: The request/response lifecycle
concepts.summary: Trace a request through the handler, the middleware chain, URL resolving, the view and rendering, and see how errors become responses.
concepts.why: Knowing each step lets you put code in the right layer and track down problems that aren't in your view.
concepts.body:
What happens between the server and your view:

1. The server calls Django's **handler**, the object at the top of `wsgi.py` or `asgi.py`: `WSGIHandler` or `ASGIHandler`. At startup the handler created every middleware once, building the chain from `MIDDLEWARE`.
2. The `request_started` signal is sent, and the handler builds an `HttpRequest` (`WSGIRequest` or `ASGIRequest`) from the raw request data the server passed in (WSGI calls it the environ, ASGI the scope).
3. The request passes **down** the middleware chain. Each layer is wrapped by `convert_exception_to_response`, so an exception raised anywhere becomes a response at that layer instead of escaping.
4. At the bottom, `_get_response` **resolves the URL**: the URL resolver for `ROOT_URLCONF` (or a per-request `request.urlconf`) returns a `ResolverMatch` holding the view, its arguments and the URL name, saved as `request.resolver_match`.
5. Middleware `process_view` hooks run, then the **view** is called (inside `atomic` if `ATOMIC_REQUESTS` is set).
6. If the view returns a `TemplateResponse`, `process_template_response` hooks run and only then is the template rendered. Because rendering waits until this point, middleware can still change the context.
7. The response travels **up** the chain. An exception runs the `process_exception` hooks, then Django's error handling: `Http404` becomes a 404 (via `handler404`), `PermissionDenied` a 403, `SuspiciousOperation` a 400, anything else a 500 (via `handler500`), and the error is written to the `django.request` log.
8. The server sends the response. When it is closed, `request_finished` fires and Django closes database connections older than `CONN_MAX_AGE`.

Streaming responses and file responses send their body bit by bit after the view has returned, so code there can't rely on things that only last for the request, such as an open transaction.
concepts.code:
# Inspecting the lifecycle from inside a project (e.g. a test or shell)
from django.core.signals import request_finished, request_started
from django.test import Client
from django.urls import resolve

match = resolve("/blog/posts/3/")
print(match.view_name, match.kwargs, match.func)    # blog:detail {'pk': 3} <function post_detail ...>

events = []
request_started.connect(lambda **kw: events.append("started"))
request_finished.connect(lambda **kw: events.append("finished"))

class ShowMatch:                                    # a middleware using process_view
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response
    def __call__(self, request):
        return self.get_response(request)
    def process_view(self, request, view_func, view_args, view_kwargs):
        events.append(f"view {request.resolver_match.view_name}")

# with ShowMatch in MIDDLEWARE:
resp = Client().get("/blog/posts/3/")
print(events)        # ['started', 'view blog:detail', 'finished']
takeaways: The handler builds the request; middleware runs down, the view runs, the response goes back up
The URL resolver produces request.resolver_match
Each middleware layer turns exceptions into responses
TemplateResponse renders after the view returns
pitfalls: Expecting process_view hooks to run for requests that a middleware higher up answered by itself.

quiz.q: A view returns a TemplateResponse. When is its template rendered?
options: After the view returns, before the response goes back up the middleware chain
Only when the response is cached
quiz.explain: TemplateResponse defers rendering so process_template_response hooks can modify it first.

concepts.name: Data migrations and zero-downtime changes
concepts.summary: Write RunPython data migrations with historical models, and change schemas safely on live databases in several steps.
concepts.why: Schema changes on busy production tables are where releases break; experts plan them in safe stages.
concepts.body:
Besides schema operations, migrations can change **data**. Create an empty one with `makemigrations blog --empty -n backfill_slugs` and add a `RunPython` operation:

```python
migrations.RunPython(forwards, backwards)
```

Inside `forwards(apps, schema_editor)`, get models with **`apps.get_model("blog", "Post")`**, never by importing them. This returns the **historical** version of the model as it was at this point in the migration history; your current `models.py` might have fields that don't exist yet. Historical models have no custom methods and no custom managers unless marked `use_in_migrations = True`. Provide a reverse function (or `RunPython.noop`) so the migration can be unapplied.

For large tables, handle rows in batches (say 1,000 at a time), and consider `atomic = False` on the migration class so a backfill doesn't hold one giant transaction. `RunSQL` runs raw SQL, and `SeparateDatabaseAndState` lets you change Django's model state without touching the database (or vice versa).

**Zero-downtime schema changes** (changes made while the site stays up) split risky operations across several deploys, because old and new code run side by side during each release:

- add a column: add it allowing NULL (or with `db_default`), deploy code that writes it, backfill, then add `NOT NULL` or constraints
- rename a column: add the new one, write both, backfill, switch reads, drop the old one later
- remove a column: stop using it in code first, then drop it in a later release

On PostgreSQL, `AddIndexConcurrently` (from `django.contrib.postgres.operations`, in a non-atomic migration) builds an index while writes to the table carry on. Always check `sqlmigrate` output for table rewrites and long locks.
concepts.code:
# blog/migrations/0007_backfill_slugs.py
from django.db import migrations
from django.utils.text import slugify

def forwards(apps, schema_editor):
    Post = apps.get_model("blog", "Post")                    # historical model
    batch = []
    for post in Post.objects.filter(slug="").only("id", "title").iterator(chunk_size=1000):
        post.slug = f"{slugify(post.title)[:40]}-{post.pk}"
        batch.append(post)
        if len(batch) == 1000:
            Post.objects.bulk_update(batch, ["slug"])
            batch.clear()
    Post.objects.bulk_update(batch, ["slug"])

class Migration(migrations.Migration):
    atomic = False                                            # no single huge transaction
    dependencies = [("blog", "0006_post_slug_nullable")]
    operations = [migrations.RunPython(forwards, migrations.RunPython.noop)]

# next release: 0008 makes slug unique and NOT NULL once all rows are filled
takeaways: RunPython with apps.get_model uses historical models, never imports
Provide reverse functions; batch large backfills, possibly with atomic = False
Split risky schema changes across releases: add, backfill, constrain, remove later
pitfalls: Importing models directly in a data migration, which breaks when the model changes later.

quiz.q: Why use apps.get_model("blog", "Post") inside a RunPython function?
options: It returns the model as it existed at that point in migration history
Imports are not allowed in migrations
quiz.explain: The historical model matches the schema at that migration, regardless of later changes to models.py.

concepts.name: Async views and the async ORM
concepts.summary: Write async views, use the async ORM methods, bridge to regular code with sync_to_async, and know the performance trade-offs.
concepts.why: Async Django can serve many requests that are mostly waiting, but only if you know where it still runs code synchronously.
concepts.body:
Django supports `async def` views. Under an **ASGI** server (Uvicorn, Daphne, Hypercorn) they run on the event loop, so one worker process can wait on many slow calls to other services at once. Under **WSGI**, async views still work, but each runs in its own one-off event loop, with no concurrency benefit.

The ORM has an **async interface**: methods prefixed with `a` (`aget`, `acreate`, `afirst`, `acount`, `aexists`, `aupdate`, `adelete`, `asave`), `async for obj in queryset`, and async versions of the related-object methods. Internally most of these still run the database **driver** (the library that talks to the database) in a thread. So they avoid blocking the event loop, but they aren't faster than regular code.

Calling code that only works synchronously (the regular ORM, many libraries) from async code raises **`SynchronousOnlyOperation`**. Wrap it with `asgiref.sync.sync_to_async(fn)`; use `async_to_sync` for the opposite direction. By default `sync_to_async` runs functions one at a time in a single shared thread (`thread_sensitive=True`) for safety, which can become the slowest point of the whole app.

Limitations to know:

- **transactions** don't work in async code; put transactional logic in a regular function and call it with `sync_to_async`
- every middleware in the list that isn't async-capable forces a hop to a thread on each request, losing much of the benefit
- following a relation lazily (`post.author`) runs a regular, synchronous query; use `select_related` or `aget`

Async views shine when one request calls several outside services at once (`asyncio.gather` with the httpx library), for streaming responses that send data bit by bit, and for long-polling, where the server holds a request open until there is news. For typical CRUD pages, regular views under WSGI remain simpler and just as fast.
concepts.code:
# blog/views.py
import asyncio
import httpx
from asgiref.sync import sync_to_async
from django.db import transaction
from django.http import JsonResponse
from .models import Post

async def post_summary(request, pk):
    post = await Post.objects.select_related("author").aget(pk=pk)
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=3) as client:
        shares, comments = await asyncio.gather(                 # concurrent I/O
            client.get(f"https://stats.example.com/shares/{pk}"),
            client.get(f"https://stats.example.com/comments/{pk}"))
    tags = [t.name async for t in post.tags.all()]
    await record_view(pk)
    return JsonResponse({"title": post.title, "author": post.author.name, "tags": tags,
                         "shares": shares.json(), "comments": comments.json()})

@sync_to_async
def record_view(pk):
    with transaction.atomic():                                   # transactions: sync only
        post = Post.objects.select_for_update().get(pk=pk)
        post.views += 1
        post.save(update_fields=["views"])
takeaways: Async views pay off under ASGI when requests spend their time waiting on I/O
Use a-prefixed ORM methods and async for; regular ORM calls raise SynchronousOnlyOperation
sync_to_async bridges to regular code, including transactions
Middleware that isn't async-capable eats into the benefit
pitfalls: Accessing a lazy relation like post.author inside an async view without select_related.

quiz.q: Inside an async view, how do you run code that needs transaction.atomic()?
options: Put it in a sync function and call it via sync_to_async
Transactions are automatic in async views
quiz.explain: Transactions aren't supported in async code yet, so the transactional code must run as regular code in a thread.
